intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina (GACR) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous (biallelic) mutation in the gene encoding ornithine aminotransferase (OAT; 613349) on chromosome 10q26.

paragraphs.text: Gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina is an autosomal recessive chorioretinal degeneration associated with hyperornithinemia and caused by deficiency of the mitochondrial matrix enzyme ornithine-delta-aminotransferase (OAT) (Valle et al., 1977; Sipila et al., 1981; Mitchell et al., 1988; Brody et al., 1992). Balfoort et al. (2021) described it as a rare inborn error of amino acid metabolism, caused by biallelic variants in the OAT gene, in which vision declines in early life and eventually leads to complete blindness, with high plasma ornithine levels. Peltola et al. (2002) listed its features as hyperornithinemia, progressive centripetal loss of vision, minor CNS abnormalities, and type II muscle fiber atrophy with accumulation of tubular aggregates. They concluded from their peripheral nerve findings that gyrate atrophy is a systemic disease affecting both the peripheral nervous system and the CNS.

paragraphs.text: Sipila et al. (1979) studied 21 patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina and hyperornithinemia. The patients were not weak. paragraphs.text: Kaiser-Kupfer et al. (1983) described cataract in 9 phakic patients with gyrate atrophy. The lens opacities lay mainly along the confluence of the posterior sutures and interfered with vision because they were in the visual axis. The authors concluded that cataract is a uniform finding in gyrate atrophy by the second decade and appears to be unique compared with cataracts associated with other forms of retinal degeneration. They examined 3 cataractous lenses removed from patients aged 31 to 47 years, both grossly and microscopically. On histology, the posterior suture region was filled with liquefied, degenerated lens material resembling typical senile cataract changes.

paragraphs.text: Valtonen et al. (1996) examined the thigh muscles of 7 patients with gyrate atrophy using semi-open conchotome muscle biopsies, CT, and ultralow-field (0.02 T) MRI. All biopsy samples showed type 2 muscle fiber atrophy, and 6 of 7 showed tubular aggregates. CT density of thigh muscle was increased in the only child studied, decreased in 3 elderly patients, and normal in the remaining 3. Compared with 6 healthy controls, mean MRI T1 relaxation times were decreased in patients (135 vs 157 ms, p = 0.002), whereas T2 was slightly but not significantly increased. The authors concluded that the thigh muscles of patients with gyrate atrophy universally show changes on CT and MRI, but that relaxation time measurements gave little additional information on muscle metabolism.

paragraphs.text: Valtonen et al. (1999) studied central nervous system involvement in 23 untreated patients with gyrate atrophy (mean age 32 +/- 18 years) and compared them with age-matched healthy controls. On brain MRI, 50% of patients had degenerative white matter lesions and 70% had premature atrophic changes, with a striking increase in the number of Virchow (perivascular) spaces. Of the patients who had an EEG, 58% had abnormal slow background activity, focal lesions, or high-amplitude beta rhythm (more than 50 microV). The EEG findings were not associated with the MRI changes or with age or sex. The authors concluded that early degenerative and atrophic brain changes and an abnormal EEG are features of gyrate atrophy, in addition to the known eye and muscle manifestations.

paragraphs.text: Sipila et al. (1980) gave intravenous arginine to 6 patients with gyrate atrophy and 6 controls. Serum arginine curves were similar in the 2 groups, but the rise in serum ornithine was more than 3 times greater in patients. Mean plasma ornithine half-time was 360 min in patients versus 97 min in controls, and patients cleared ornithine from the extracellular fluid significantly more slowly. Patients always excreted less guanidinoacetate than controls, with highly significant differences within each sex. Differences in creatine excretion were less marked.

paragraphs.text: Balfoort et al. (2021) performed a systematic review of therapeutic interventions in gyrate atrophy following PRISMA guidelines. They identified 33 studies covering 107 patients, mostly case reports (27) or case series (4), and found no randomized controlled trials or large cohort studies. Protein-restricted diets lowered ornithine levels by 16.0 to 91.2%, and lysine supplementation lowered them by 21 to 34%. Pyridoxine responsiveness was reported in 30% of the included mutations. Other reported treatments were creatine or creatine precursor supplementation and proline supplementation. The authors concluded that a protein-restricted diet, pyridoxine supplementation (depending on the variant), and/or lysine supplementation can reduce ornithine levels. Because the included studies lacked predefined clinical outcome measures and structured follow-up, however, they could not draw conclusions about clinical effectiveness. They noted that there is no curative treatment and no international treatment protocol.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1995) produced OAT-deficient mice by gene targeting. As neonates the mice had hypoornithinemia and died, but short-term arginine supplementation rescued them. After weaning they developed hyperornithinemia similar to that of human patients with gyrate atrophy. Over several months they developed a retinal degeneration involving the photoreceptors and pigment epithelium. The authors concluded that OAT-deficient mice appear to be an excellent model of the human disease.

paragraphs.text: Mitchell et al. (1988) studied 4 Lebanese patients with gyrate atrophy from 2 pedigrees. RNase A protection with antisense RNA probes showed a probe-target mismatch at the 5-prime end of the first coding exon of the OAT gene. PCR amplification and sequencing of genomic DNA identified a G-to-A transition that changed the initiator ATG (methionine) codon to ATA, and the mutation segregated with the gyrate atrophy allele in both pedigrees. If translation began at the nearest in-frame methionine codon, OAT would be truncated by 138 amino acids, losing the entire mitochondrial leader sequence and 113 amino acids of the mature peptide.
